title: Hymn and Room
premise: Lena Pemberton returns to the drowned village of Ashmoor to bury his twin sister, only to find the residents insisting she is still alive and the church bell—melted down in 1911—ringing each dusk. The village is a living ritual: the founders bound a hungry presence beneath the chapel, and every resident who 'signs the papers' becomes a keeper, their memories rewritten to feed it. Lena, invisible since childhood, is the one keeper the ritual never claimed. As the last elderly resident prepares to sign, the bell rings louder and the village begins forgetting itself. Lena must finish the founders' ritual—naming every soul the bell has swallowed, including his sister—freeing Ashmoor at the cost of his own memories of her, and chooses to stay as its final, willing keeper.
about_author: Ansel Sandoval is the pen name of a former church archivist from coastal New England who spent a decade cataloguing parish records from villages that no longer appear on maps. Hymn and Room is his third novel, written in a house he refuses to describe.

chapters.title: The Wrong Sibling
chapters.summary: Lena arrives in Ashmoor with his sister's ashes, but the funeral director greets him by her name, Mara, and the guestbook already holds her signature. His POV establishes his habit of counting doors and lights. Emotional beat: disorientation—the grief he brought doesn't fit the grief he finds.

chapters.title: Bell Weather
chapters.summary: At dusk the church bell rings, though the archive confirms it was melted in 1911. The villagers pause mid-motion, then resume, unbothered. Old resident Edith Corrow warns Lena never to answer a bell after dark. Emotional beat: dread sharpening into resolve as Lena realizes the village runs on rules no one will state aloud.

chapters.title: The Papers
chapters.summary: Lena finds a ledger of 'signatures' dating to 1849—every resident, each entry followed by a small notation: remembered, or kept. His sister's name is there, unsigned. He begins investigating the founders' ritual through the chapel crypt. Emotional beat: the investigator's thrill curdling as the ledger's logic becomes clear.

chapters.title: What Edith Kept
chapters.summary: Edith, the last unsigned resident, shows Lena her childhood: a twin brother the village no longer remembers, taken by the bell. She reveals the ritual requires a keeper who remembers what the village forgets. Emotional beat: found-family tenderness between two people the village has tried to erase.

chapters.title: Doors That Weren't Counted
chapters.summary: The house grows a thirteenth door overnight. Inside, Lena finds his sister's room intact, her handwriting on the walls—warnings, or invitations. The village's memory of Mara begins rewriting itself around him. Emotional beat: guilt and hope tangled; he may have buried the wrong twin because he was meant to.

chapters.title: Hymn for the Drowned
chapters.summary: In the flooded crypt, Lena recovers the founders' hymnal: the ritual is a sung census, every swallowed soul must be named aloud. The bell rings during the attempt, and something answers in his sister's voice. Emotional beat: longing weaponized—the presence knows exactly what to impersonate.

chapters.title: The Last Signature
chapters.summary: Edith, worn down by the bell, decides to sign and end her remembering. Lena begs her to wait; she refuses, saying some truths are heavier than loyalty. She signs at dawn and forgets him by noon. Emotional beat: betrayal that is also mercy—the theme of loyalty versus truth made flesh.

chapters.title: Counting Backwards
chapters.summary: With Edith signed, the village accelerates its forgetting: houses vanish, the door count fails, villagers begin ringing the bell themselves. Lena realizes the ritual is failing and the presence will be unbound entirely. Emotional beat: panic and clarity—he is the last keeper whether he signs or not.

chapters.title: The Census of Ashmoor
chapters.summary: In the chapel, Lena sings the founders' hymn and names every soul in the ledger—generations of the kept—ending with Mara. The bell cracks; the presence, finally witnessed, is released into memory instead of hunger. He sees his sister once, whole, before the naming takes his memories of her. Emotional beat: cathartic grief, sacrifice as love.

chapters.title: Keeper of the Quiet
chapters.summary: Ashmoor stands ordinary and bell-less; the residents remember nothing, but they keep Lena's lights on and count his doors for him. He finds Edith's unsigned page in his pocket and a hymnal he can no longer read, and stays willingly. Emotional beat: quiet, bittersweet resolution—found family built on a shared forgetting.
